face-slimming-supplements-teas.summary: Herbal teas and capsules taken for a leaner, less puffy face through diuretic, appetite or detox effects.

quick.overview:
Face slimming teas and capsules are herbal products people take hoping for less facial puffiness and a leaner-looking face. The payoff they are after is a slimmer jawline and cheeks with less morning swelling.

The chain marketers describe runs through diuretic, laxative, appetite or metabolism effects: less water and less overall body fat, which can show in the face. No trial has tested these products for facial fat, and research on fat loss generally reports that it is not targeted to one body area. In the US, herbal teas need to be safe to consume but are not required to show they work.
quick.how: People drink the teas or take the capsules daily as a routine alongside dieting, and some use them for a short stretch before photos or events. Users commonly pair them with calorie control, lower salt intake and exercise, since overall leanness is what shows in the face. Reported timelines vary by product and by how much weight a person is also losing.
quick.risks: Documented concerns with herbal weight-loss products include contamination and drug interactions with some herbs. Ephedra-containing supplements were banned in the US in 2004. Diuretic and laxative ingredients can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss. Products vary widely in content, and people taking medication or with heart or kidney conditions are commonly advised to check with a clinician first.

angle.text: Users take herbal slimming teas and capsules hoping for a leaner, less puffy face, through diuretic, laxative or detox effects that reduce water and body fat. The face-specific payoff comes from general weight-loss marketing, and no trial has tested these products for facial fat.

ketogenic-diet-face.summary: A very low-carb diet that appearance communities use to lean out cheeks and cut puffiness through fat loss and less water retention.

quick.overview:
People use a ketogenic diet to get a leaner, less puffy face: slimmer cheeks, a sharper jaw and less bloat. The face gets leaner as overall body fat comes down and water retention drops.

Cutting carbohydrate makes the liver produce ketone bodies for fuel, and low-carb diets can produce somewhat greater short-term weight loss than low-fat diets. A 2022 Cochrane review found no weight-loss advantage over balanced diets at two years. The diet was developed in the 1920s for epilepsy, and no study has measured facial appearance on it.
quick.how: People follow it as a long-running eating pattern: high fat, moderate protein, very few carbohydrates, usually tracked with food logs or ketone strips. It is often combined with lifting or cardio and with a calorie deficit. Many users report noticing less bloat within the first couple of weeks, with fat-loss changes in the face taking longer as body fat drops.
quick.risks: Reported effects include constipation, raised cholesterol, nutrient gaps and, rarely, ketoacidosis. It is contraindicated in certain metabolic disorders. People with diabetes on medication, kidney or liver disease, or who are pregnant are generally advised to get medical input before starting.

angle.text: Appearance communities use a ketogenic diet to lean out the cheeks and reduce puffiness: very low carbohydrate intake leads to fat loss and lower water retention, which shows in the face. Weight-loss studies exist for the diet, and facial appearance specifically has not been measured.

omad-36-hour-fasts.summary: Eating once a day or fasting 36 hours between meals to cut body fat fast and reveal a leaner face.

quick.overview:
OMAD (one meal a day) packs all eating into a window of an hour or two, and 36-hour fasts leave a day and a half between meals. People use them to drop body fat quickly and get a leaner face with less bloat.

The pattern works mainly by lowering total calorie intake, and the fat loss that results shows in the face as it shows elsewhere. Most human studies of intermittent fasting report weight loss of roughly 2.5 to 9.9 percent, and some reviews show results similar to ordinary calorie restriction. Health bodies including the American Heart Association and the US National Institute on Aging describe the evidence as limited or inconclusive. Weight lost includes some lean mass.
quick.how: People pick a daily eating window or fast on set days, drinking water, black coffee or tea in between and eating one large meal, often high in protein. It is commonly paired with lifting to hold on to muscle. Results show as steady scale and mirror changes over weeks, depending on the calorie deficit.
quick.risks: Reported effects include hunger, dizziness, headaches and irritability. Fasting is not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults or people prone to eating disorders, and prolonged fasts raise gallstone risk. Some lean mass is lost along with fat.

angle.text: Users eat one meal a day or fast for 36 hours to build a calorie deficit, lose body fat quickly and reveal a leaner face. Intermittent fasting trials show weight loss, with facial leanness following from overall fat loss rather than being measured directly.

cardio-zone-2-for-leanness.summary: Steady low-intensity aerobic exercise that burns calories and lowers body fat for a leaner face and body.

quick.overview:
Zone 2 cardio is steady, conversational-pace aerobic exercise, commonly placed at roughly 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate. People use it to burn calories and lower body fat, aiming for a leaner face and body without hard training that cuts into lifting recovery.

At this intensity fat is the main fuel, and sources report that aerobic exercise promotes weight loss, with fat loss being a whole-body result of energy balance rather than targeted to one area. Public-health bodies recommend about 2.5 hours of moderate aerobic exercise a week for health. High-intensity intervals can deliver similar benefits in less time, and zone 2 has no universally accepted definition.
quick.how: People walk briskly on an incline, cycle, row or use an elliptical for 30 to 60 minutes several times a week, often on non-lifting days or after training. It is combined with a calorie deficit and strength work. Body-fat changes build over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Reported risks include overuse injury, overtraining, and low-energy-availability problems in high-volume athletes who under-fuel. People with heart conditions or who are new to exercise are commonly advised to build up gradually.

angle.text: Users do steady low-intensity cardio to burn calories and lower body fat, which brings a leaner face and body into view. Aerobic exercise is well studied for health and weight, and zone 2 specifically for leanness is still debated.

water-fasting.summary: Multi-day zero-calorie fasting used for rapid fat loss and a leaner face, with some users also reporting skin changes.

quick.overview:
Water fasting means taking no calories for a day or more, usually several days. People use it for rapid fat loss and a leaner face, and some say their skin looks clearer.

With no intake, the body draws on glycogen and then protein and fat, and shifts toward ketone use for the brain over days. Physiology sources report that a large share of early weight loss in a prolonged fast is lean tissue, and studies cover shorter intermittent fasts rather than repeated extended ones. Some users report hair shedding afterward.
quick.how: People fast on water, sometimes with added electrolytes, for a set number of days and then reintroduce food gradually. It is usually done as an occasional reset rather than a routine, and some users follow it with a structured diet. Scale changes appear within days, though early drops include water and lean tissue.
quick.risks: Documented risks include electrolyte loss, gallstones and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal and can occur after about 4 to 5 days without food. Fasting is not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults or people prone to eating disorders.

angle.text: Users fast on water for days to create a large calorie deficit, dropping body fat quickly for a leaner face, with some claims about skin as well. Fasting studies cover weight and metabolic markers, and the skin and facial effects come from user reports.

t3-thyroid-fat-loss.summary: Off-label use of the thyroid hormone liothyronine (T3) to raise metabolic rate and shed body fat while cutting.

quick.overview:
T3 is the active thyroid hormone, available by prescription as liothyronine for hypothyroidism. In bodybuilding and cutting circles it has been used off-label to raise metabolic rate and lose body fat for a leaner look.

T3 raises basal metabolic rate, affects protein synthesis and increases sensitivity to catecholamines such as adrenaline. The prescribing label states that in people with normal thyroid function, ordinary hormone-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction and that larger doses can cause serious toxicity. No published trial of T3 as a cosmetic fat-loss method was found.
quick.how: Use is described mainly in bodybuilding contexts during short cutting phases, alongside calorie restriction and training, and usually discussed as a prescription-only drug obtained through a clinician. Reported timelines are weeks.
quick.risks: Excess thyroid hormone can cause sweating, tremor, insomnia, arrhythmias and heart failure. The label warns of serious or life-threatening toxicity at larger doses, especially alongside sympathomimetic amines. It can also suppress the body's own thyroid function. It is prescription-only in the UK and Canada.

angle.text: Users take the thyroid hormone T3 off-label during cutting phases to raise metabolic rate and shed body fat for a leaner look. The drug is approved for hypothyroidism, and its label states that normal-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction in people with normal thyroid function.

ephedrine-eca-stack.summary: A stimulant stack of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin used while cutting to raise metabolism, curb appetite and drop fat.

quick.overview:
ECA stands for ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It has long been popular with bodybuilders cutting fat before competitions, and a looksmax.org guide describes it as a stack for raising metabolism, suppressing appetite and adding energy.

Ephedrine triggers release of norepinephrine, activating adrenergic receptors, and also slows gastric emptying; caffeine and related compounds are reported to act synergistically with it. A 2021 systematic review found ephedrine, with or without caffeine, produced about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks. Long-term effects are unknown.
quick.how: Users take it during cutting phases alongside a calorie deficit and training, often for limited stretches. Guides pair it with exercise for a leaner physique, and effects on appetite and energy are felt the same day.
quick.risks: Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, tremor, rapid heart rate, arrhythmias and hypertension; stroke and heart attack are serious risks, and a forum guide itself warns against use with heart problems. The FDA banned ephedrine alkaloid supplements in 2004, and legal status varies by country.

angle.text: Bodybuilders and looksmaxxers use the ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin stack to raise metabolism and curb appetite when cutting, leading to fat loss and a leaner physique. Trials have found modest short-term fat loss.

dnp-2-4-dinitrophenol.summary: An industrial chemical that burns energy as heat, pursued for very fast fat loss; banned for human use since 1938 and tied to documented deaths.

quick.overview:
DNP is an industrial chemical sold as a diet drug in the 1930s and withdrawn after reports of cataracts, blindness and deaths. It has resurfaced online, where bodybuilders and others on looksmaxxing forums describe using it for very fast fat loss and an extremely lean look.

DNP acts as a protonophore: it lets protons leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, so energy that would have made ATP is released as heat and metabolic rate rises. Users on forums report large weight losses over a few weeks, with heat, sweating and fever. Evidence on its effects in humans comes mainly from 1930s clinical reports, toxicology and poison-centre case data.
quick.how: Forum users describe multi-week courses during cuts, often combined with other substances and with dieting. Regulators and clinicians describe a narrow gap between effective and toxic exposure.
quick.risks: Documented harms include dangerously high body temperature, cataracts, nerve damage and death, with no specific antidote; overdose causes fatal hyperthermia. It was judged too toxic for human consumption under the 1938 US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, is banned for human consumption in many countries, has been prohibited by WADA since 2015, and was reclassified as a regulated poison in the UK in 2023.

angle.text: Some forum users pursue DNP for very fast fat loss over a few weeks: it makes mitochondria release food energy as heat, burning calories quickly for a leaner body and face. It was marketed for weight loss in the 1930s, and regulators and clinicians document fatalities.

fat-grafting-for-facial-asymmetry.summary: Surgeons move your own fat into the thinner side of the face to even out volume and give a fuller, more balanced look.

quick.overview:
Fat grafting harvests a patient's own fat, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas lacking volume. For asymmetry, the payoff is a visibly fuller, more even face once the thinner side is built up to match.

The fat is washed or filtered and re-injected into the target area. Facial fat grafting is widely used in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery. A systematic review reports that a main drawback is high and unpredictable absorption, so surgeons judge retention from experience; the studies reviewed concern facial volume restoration in general rather than asymmetry specifically.
quick.how: It is done by a surgeon, often under sedation or anaesthesia, with fat taken from areas such as the abdomen or thighs. Swelling settles over weeks and the final volume shows after some of the graft is absorbed. Because retention varies, some patients have repeat sessions.
quick.risks: Reported problems include swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, fat necrosis and reabsorption; a systematic review asks whether facial fat grafting is worth its risk. Results may need touch-ups.

angle.text: Surgeons move a patient's own fat into the thinner side of the face so the two sides match in volume, giving a visibly fuller, more balanced face. Fat transfer is a standard reconstructive and aesthetic technique, with graft survival varying between patients.

ptosis-surgery-for-asymmetry.summary: Eyelid surgery that lifts a drooping upper lid so both eyes open to a similar height and look more alike.

quick.overview:
Ptosis is a drooping upper eyelid. Surgery raises the lower-set lid so the eyes look more alike and more open, and in looksmaxxing discussions it is cited as a way to fix eye asymmetry.

Techniques include shortening the levator muscle, resecting Muller's muscle, or suspending the lid from the forehead muscle (frontalis sling) when the lid muscle is very weak. Surgical series describe it as an established treatment for mild to severe ptosis, with outcomes that vary by cause and technique, and case series of minimally invasive suspension report short recovery.
quick.how: It is performed by an oculoplastic or eyelid surgeon, usually under local anaesthesia, with the technique matched to how weak the lid muscle is. Swelling and bruising settle over a few weeks and the result is visible once healed.
quick.risks: Reported complications include uneven lids after surgery, dry eye if the eye does not close fully, bleeding, infection, rarely loss of lid movement, and recurrence. Underlying causes such as myasthenia gravis are assessed separately.

angle.text: Eyelid surgery lifts a lower-set upper lid so both eyes open to a similar height and look more alike and more open. It is an established procedure for ptosis, and the change is visible once healed.

bilateral-chewing-habit.summary: Deliberately alternating the chewing side so jaw muscles and face shape stay even from left to right.

quick.overview:
The practice is to chew evenly on both sides of the mouth instead of favouring one. People do it hoping to keep the jaw muscles and face symmetrical, on the premise that one-sided chewing could contribute to facial asymmetry.

Chewing is mostly unconscious, though conscious input can influence it, and feedback from nerves in the teeth and jaw joints helps control how forcefully each muscle works. The pattern adapts to the food and to changes in the teeth. The link between chewing side and facial symmetry is a community theory, and no studies were found testing it.
quick.how: People simply switch sides as they eat, sometimes counting bites or alternating by mouthful, until it becomes habit. It costs nothing and is usually combined with other symmetry habits. Any change in face shape would be gradual, over months or years.
quick.risks: No documented harms were found for this practice. Tooth pain, missing teeth, jaw joint problems or dentures can change which side a person chews on, and a dentist can assess those.

angle.text: Users alternate the chewing side to load both jaw muscles evenly, hoping to keep the jaw and face shape balanced left to right. The link from chewing side to facial symmetry is a community theory, and no studies were found on it.

unilateral-chewing-correction.summary: Chewing on both sides to correct a one-sided habit that people blame for a lopsided jaw or cheek.

quick.overview:
Unilateral chewing correction means consciously alternating the chewing side, or favouring the less-used side, to break a habit of chewing mostly on one. In looksmaxxing circles that habit is sometimes blamed for uneven jaw or cheek development, so the goal is a more symmetrical face.

The proposed idea is that the masseter and tissue on the chewing side are loaded more, so that over years the face develops unevenly, and corrective practice equalises the loading. Dental research confirms most people have a preferred chewing side and has studied how it relates to handedness, bite pattern and jaw joint factors. No published study has tested whether changing it alters facial appearance.
quick.how: It is a free habit change: people notice which side they default to and deliberately use the other, sometimes with reminders, until both sides are used. Any effect would be expected over a long period.
quick.risks: Alternating the chewing side is an ordinary behaviour with no documented harms in the literature reviewed. Tooth pain, missing teeth, jaw joint problems or dentures can change which side a person chews on, and clinicians assess those causes separately.

angle.text: People who chew mostly on one side switch to using both sides, aiming to even out the load on the jaw muscles and reduce a lopsided jaw or cheek. It is a free habit change, and no study has tested whether it alters facial symmetry.

flipped-mirror-selfie-check.summary: Comparing your mirror-reversed face with a true photo to see the face others see and choose better angles and styling.

quick.overview:
A flipped mirror selfie check compares the mirror view of your face, the one you see daily, with a non-mirrored photo, which is closer to how other people see you. The payoff is seeing which features and angles look different, so you can pick better photo angles and styling.

A mirror shows a left-right reversed image, and phone cameras may save either orientation. The idea draws on the mere-exposure effect, in which people feel more familiar with the view they see most often. Facial symmetry research uses fluctuating asymmetry as its main measure and has associated greater symmetry with higher attractiveness ratings. The flipped-selfie practice itself has not been studied.
quick.how: Users take a selfie, view it in both orientations, often side by side, and note which features and angles change. They use this when choosing profile photos, hair parting and grooming. It takes a few minutes and needs only a phone.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Community discussions note that comparing mirrored views can feed preoccupation with small asymmetries.

angle.text: Users compare a mirror-reversed face with a non-reversed photo to see the face others see, since familiarity with the mirror image shapes self-perception. This helps with angle and styling choices, and draws on familiarity effects described in psychology.

symmetry-photo-mirroring-tools.summary: Apps and editors that build left-left and right-right face composites from one photo so you can see exactly how your two sides differ.

quick.overview:
Symmetry photo mirroring tools take a front-facing photo, split it down the midline and mirror each half to create two composite faces, one built from two left sides and one from two right sides. Users compare them with the original to see how their two sides differ, which helps inform styling or treatment choices.

The same technique appears in academic research on facial symmetry and attractiveness, where face halves are mirrored and blended. Critics note that mirroring can create artificial features; for example a slightly bent nose can appear oversized or unnaturally small depending on which side is copied.
quick.how: Users upload or open a straight-on, evenly lit photo, mark the midline and generate both composites, then compare them with the original. Results depend on midline placement and on head rotation and tilt, so people retake photos for consistency. It takes minutes.
quick.risks: No physical risk. Because the composites exaggerate or hide particular features, the method has been criticised as a basis for conclusions about a face.

angle.text: Apps and editors build left-left and right-right composites from one photo so users can see exactly how their two sides differ, and use that to inform styling or treatment choices. The composites are an established research method with known artefacts.

back-sleeping-pillow-setup.summary: Using pillows to stay on your back at night, which users hope avoids one-sided facial pressure and uneven looks.

quick.overview:
A back sleeping pillow setup uses pillows beside the body or under the neck and knees to discourage rolling onto the side or face. Users adopt it hoping to avoid overnight pressure on one side of the face and the asymmetry, wrinkles or flattening they associate with side sleeping.

Pillows act as barriers or supports so the sleeper stays supine. The community theory is that continuous pressure on one side during sleep affects soft tissue or skeletal development over time. On looksmax.org, posters describe attributing a worse-looking side to the side they sleep on, while other replies attribute asymmetry to genetics. No study has tested pillow arrangements for changing facial appearance.
quick.how: People wedge pillows along both sides of the torso, add a neck-support pillow and sometimes one under the knees, and give themselves some nights to get used to it. Some use it with a flat, supportive face-up position through the night.
quick.risks: Sleep literature associates back sleeping with positional obstructive sleep apnea in a large share of OSA cases and with more frequent sleep paralysis; positional therapy that discourages back sleeping is used for apnea. People who snore or have apnea may want to check this with a clinician.

angle.text: Users arrange pillows to stay on their back, aiming to avoid one-sided facial pressure and uneven looks building up over time. The belief rests on forum reports about sleep side, and sleep position effects on facial shape have not been studied.

chiropractic-neck-adjustment.summary: A quick thrust applied to neck joints, sometimes sought for better posture, head alignment and a more balanced profile.

quick.overview:
A chiropractic neck adjustment is a thrust applied to the joints of the cervical spine, usually by a chiropractor. In appearance communities it is sought for better head and neck posture, and occasionally for jaw or face alignment, aiming for a more balanced profile.

A quick, small-amplitude thrust is applied to a cervical joint, often producing a popping sound, and practitioners say it restores joint movement. Research on cervical manipulation concerns neck pain: a 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence, while a smaller body of moderate-to-low-quality evidence suggests multiple sessions may improve pain and function compared with some medications. No study evaluates it for facial appearance.
quick.how: People book sessions with a chiropractor, often a series, sometimes alongside posture exercises. A session takes minutes and the thrust is felt immediately.
quick.risks: The main concern is vertebral artery dissection, which can lead to stroke; case reports also describe cerebellar infarction and preretinal hemorrhages after neck manipulation. A 2001 study reported higher rates of vertebrobasilar stroke in adults under 45 who had recently visited a chiropractor, with no significant association over 45, and some chiropractors dispute a causal link.

angle.text: Some appearance communities seek neck adjustments to improve head and neck posture and alignment, hoping for a more balanced profile. Manipulation has been studied for neck pain, and an appearance effect has not been tested.

craniosacral-therapy.summary: Light-touch manual therapy on the head, spine and sacrum, tried by some in the hope of shifting skull bones and improving facial symmetry.

quick.overview:
Craniosacral therapy (CST) is an alternative manual therapy in which a practitioner uses light touch on the head, spine and sacrum to detect and adjust a rhythm said to travel through the cerebrospinal fluid. A few looksmaxxing posters try it hoping to adjust skull bones, bite and posture for better facial symmetry.

It grew out of cranial osteopathy by William Sutherland and was developed by John Upledger. Proponents hold that skull bones move in a cycle at roughly 6 to 12 cycles per minute and that therapists can feel and release restrictions. Studies have found practitioners cannot reliably identify the rhythm, systematic reviews report limited evidence, and medical reviews describe the premise as inconsistent with anatomy.
quick.how: Clients lie clothed on a table while the practitioner holds the head, neck and lower back with light pressure, typically over a series of sessions of 30 to 60 minutes.
quick.risks: Reviews describe manipulation of the skull as potentially harmful, particularly for infants and children, and report at least two deaths linked to CST spinal manipulation as of 2018. The American Cancer Society advises against use on children under two, and using it as the only treatment for serious illness has been cautioned against.

angle.text: Some users try craniosacral therapy hoping that light touch on the skull and spine will adjust skull bones and improve facial symmetry. The therapy rests on a claimed cranial rhythm, and reviews report limited evidence of benefit.

myofascial-release-rolfing.summary: Hands-on fascia work, best known as Rolfing, used to realign posture and the body and, in some circles, the face.

quick.overview:
Rolfing, formally Structural Integration, is a manual therapy created by biochemist Ida Rolf. It is usually a series of ten sessions of slow, deep pressure on connective tissue (fascia) with movement cues, and practitioners say it brings the body into better alignment with gravity for better posture and a more balanced look. In looksmaxxing circles it is also raised as a way to balance facial structure.

Proponents hold that gravity and injury shorten and thicken fascia, and that manual pressure lengthens it and restores balance; researchers say this mechanism has not been validated in large controlled studies. Published research has examined posture, neck function and pain, and a 2024 systematic review rated the evidence very low certainty. An Australian government review in 2015 found no clear evidence of effectiveness.
quick.how: People book a practitioner for a structured series, or use broader myofascial release such as massage-style pressure and foam rolling. Sessions combine deep pressure with guided movement over weeks.
quick.risks: Sessions can be painful and leave soreness. Case reports describe harm from deep massage in unusual circumstances, such as displacement of a ureteral stent. Rolfing is not a regulated medical treatment in most places.

angle.text: Practitioners offer Rolfing and myofascial release to change tissue tension and realign posture and the body, and in some circles the face, for a more balanced look. Trials exist for pain and function with low-certainty results, and no study has examined facial appearance.

tmj-splint-orthotic.summary: A custom dental splint worn to stabilize or reposition the jaw joint, discussed for jaw alignment and a more balanced face.

quick.overview:
A TMJ splint is a removable acrylic appliance, usually custom-made by a dentist, that fits over the upper or lower teeth. In looksmaxxing circles the idea is that correcting jaw-joint imbalance can improve bite, jaw symmetry and facial balance.

Stabilization splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to relax the jaw muscles and spread bite forces. Repositioning splints hold the lower jaw in a different position, for example forward, to try to improve how the joint disc sits while worn. Studies focus on pain and joint function, and reviews describe modest evidence for hard stabilization splints in TMD pain and insufficient evidence on other points; appearance outcomes have not been researched.
quick.how: A dentist takes impressions and fits the splint, which is typically worn at night or for set periods, with follow-up adjustments. Use is generally considered reversible.
quick.risks: Partial-coverage splints can cause unwanted tooth movement, and orthodontic literature describes posterior open bites after repositioning splint therapy, which can need orthodontic work. Fit and use are monitored by the dentist.

angle.text: Users interested in jaw alignment discuss custom splints that stabilize or reposition the jaw joint, hoping for a more even bite and a more balanced face. Splints are used for TMJ disorders with modest evidence, and appearance outcomes have not been researched.

tmj-botox.summary: Botulinum toxin injected into jaw muscles to relax clenching and jaw pain, with masseter treatment also giving some users a slimmer lower face.

quick.overview:
TMJ Botox refers to injecting botulinum toxin into jaw muscles, such as the masseter or lateral pterygoid, to calm overactive muscles in people with temporomandibular disorders or teeth grinding. Users also seek it for a slimmer, softer lower face, since weakening the masseter reduces its bulk, and for more even jaw muscles.

Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at nerve endings, temporarily weakening the injected muscle. In TMD the rationale is that lateral pterygoid spasm may contribute to anterior disc displacement. Multiple randomized trials of lateral pterygoid injection report benefit, while a set of newer registered trials is small and results are mixed in the sources.
quick.how: A clinician injects the muscles in a short visit, and it is a prescription treatment. Effects typically last months, so people repeat it periodically, with changes building over a few weeks.
quick.risks: Toxin spread can cause a fixed facial expression that resolves as the effect wears off. Use for TMD is generally off-label. Pregnant or breastfeeding people and those with certain neuromuscular conditions are commonly advised to avoid it.

angle.text: Botulinum toxin in the jaw muscles is used for clenching and jaw pain, and users also seek it for a slimmer lower face or more even jaw muscles as the treated masseter shrinks. Facial slimming is a recognized effect of treating the masseter, and the symmetry use is off-label.
